title: Mortality of \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\) of \(2\times 2\) integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist \(\ell\)\(\ge 1\) and indices \(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{\ell}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(A_{i_{1}} A_{i_{2}} \cdots  A_{i_{\ell}}=0_{2}\)?
why: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.

progress.text: The two-dimensional integer mortality problem is shown NP-hard; lower-bound attribution checked in later primary papers.
The revised affine-reachability paper proves NP-completeness under the determinant promise {0,+1}.
The same authors explicitly retain general two-dimensional mortality as open while resolving membership complexity for \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\).
New results concern word representations and embeddings in complex matrix structures rather than unrestricted integer mortality.

definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: Can a sequence erase every vector?
context_blocks.text: A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

context_blocks.title: Two small examples
context_blocks.text: Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: Hardness and undecidability are different claims
context_blocks.text: Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

context_blocks.title: Restricted matrix classes have stronger results
context_blocks.text: Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other matrix questions
context_blocks.text: General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

sentences: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition.
The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix.
Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted.
NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case.
Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.
